youtube.description: In this episode you will share one value among all objects, write a static member function and know that static functions have no this, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Static members · 1:21 Count the objects · 2:18 One shared copy · 2:51 Second program · 3:55 Recap · 4:25 Bug of the Day · 5:24 Challenge · 5:50 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we share data between objects. A static member belongs to the class, and every object sees the same one.

scenes.onScreen: "Static members": numbered lines (1. A static member belongs to the class; 2. All objects share one copy; 3. A static function has no this) and an analogy card: a school notice board: one board, shared by every classroom
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A normal member belongs to each object. A static member belongs to the class. There is only one copy, and every object shares it. Since C plus plus seventeen, you can write inline static and set the value inside the class. A static function has no this pointer, so it can only use static members. Think of a school notice board. There is one board, and every classroom reads it. Static members are useful for shared facts. How many tickets were sold? What is the tax rate? These facts belong to the class, not to one object. You reach a static member with the class name and two colons. You do not need an object.
points: A static member belongs to the class
A static function has no this

analogy.title: Static members
analogy.body: A school notice board: one board, shared by every classroom

scenes.onScreen: tally.cpp: a static counter counts how many objects exist
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 6] Sold is static. It belongs to the class, and there is one copy. [HL 7] Each constructor adds one to the shared count. [HL 11] Three objects are made, so the count goes up three times. [HL 12] We reach a static member with the class name and two colons. The answer is three. [HL 6] The static member is made once, for the whole class. The word inline gives it its value inside the class. [HL 7] Each constructor adds one to the shared count. [HL 11] Three objects are made, so the constructor runs three times. [HL 12] The class name and two colons reach the count. The answer is three.

scenes.onScreen: three objects, and one static value in the static region
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: Look at the static region. One box holds sold. The three objects do not each have their own copy. They all read and write the same box. Notice that the three objects have their own data, but they share one counter. The counter lives in the static region, so it stays until the program ends.

scenes.onScreen: statfunc.cpp: a static function works without an object
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 6] A static function belongs to the class. We can call it without an object. [HL 10] We write the class name, two colons, and the function name. One hundred degrees Celsius is two hundred twelve degrees Fahrenheit. [HL 6] A static function does not need an object. It works only with its parameters and with other static members. [HL 10] We call it with the class name. The answer for one hundred degrees is two hundred and twelve.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as statfunc dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints two hundred twelve. Notice that no Temperature object exists in this program. The function still works.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A static member belongs to the class. Two. All objects share one copy. Three. Reach it with the class name and two colons. Four. A static function has no this pointer. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A static member belongs to the class.
Reach it with the class name and two colons.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A static function that uses a normal member
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. A static function tries to read a normal member. The compiler says invalid use of member in static member function. A static function has no object, so it has no count. Make the function normal, and call it on an object. A static function has no object behind it, so it has no this pointer. A normal member belongs to an object, and none exists. The compiler cannot decide which count to read. Make the member static too, or make the function normal.

scenes.onScreen: Why is the static member so popular? Everybody shares it, and nobody pays rent.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why is the static member so popular? Everybody shares it, and nobody pays rent.

scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a class with a static counter. Count how many objects exist. Print the count after you make five. Hint: add one to the static counter in the constructor, and print it after five objects. Write your answer in the comments.

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

statfunc.cpp: In static member function 'static int Counter::peek()':
statfunc.cpp:8:32: error: invalid use of member 'Counter::count_' in static member function
    8 |     static int peek() { return count_; }
      |                                ^~~~~~
statfunc.cpp:5:9: note: declared here
    5 |     int count_ = 0;
bug.why: A normal member belongs to an object. A static function has no object, so it has no count to read.
